description: We are a team of five passionate students participating in NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026. Our challenge is “Abandoned but not Forgotten.” We aim to bring NASA's discarded equipment on the Moon and Mars back to life through engaging digital storytelling. Using creativity, technology, and NASA data, we want to explore the history, purpose, and scientific importance of these forgotten objects. Our goal is to make space exploration history interesting, interactive, and accessible to everyone.
summary:
AUREX-Exploring Humanity's Footprints on the Moon and Mars

Humanity's journey into space has left behind more than scientific achievements; it has created a remarkable history of exploration, discovery and technological progress. AUREX 2.0 is an interactive space-exploration platform that brings this history closer to everyone by presenting NASA's lunar and Martian missions through a unified digital experience.

The platform features 13 missions — 7 lunar and 6 Martian missions — enabling users to discover historic and robotic explorations, including Apollo 11, Curiosity and Viking. Its mission-search functionality helps users navigate and discover missions using names and keywords. Integrating NASA's Image and Video Library, AUREX also connects mission exploration with authentic space imagery and visual resources.

Mission information is compiled from NASA's official mission pages, while its multimedia resources draw on NASA's publicly accessible image and video collections. By combining mission discovery, historical context, search functionality and space-related visual content, AUREX transforms scattered exploration records into an accessible and engaging learning experience.

Its central vision is simple:make humanity's exploration of two neighbouring worlds easier to discover, understand and appreciate — while preserving the scientific and historical significance of every mission.

This is an independent project and is not officially affiliated with or endorsed by NASA.
details:
1. What does it do, and how does it work?

A visitor sees the Moon and Mars as two large planet buttons over a drawn space scene. Tapping a planet lists every mission to it. Each mission has its own page, which includes:

Status label: Active, Completed, Inactive, Crashed or Intentionally left. Tapping it opens a page explaining why, with the hardware's last report and where it rests today.

Detailed explanation: it answers six questions about the hardware itself. Was it left on purpose? Did it crash, and was it lost? Did it finish its mission? Has it stopped working? Can NASA still control it? Is it in space or on a surface?

Question pages: each question opens a page with a full explanation. Tapping a person's name leads to their profile, with a biography and age.

Photo gallery: official NASA photographs open one at a time, with description, date, photographer and a link back to NASA's own record.

Quiz: Level 1 has 25 easy questions. Scoring 80 points unlocks Level 2, with 25 tougher ones. Every option explains why it is right or wrong.

Aurex 2.0 assistant: the student asks a question in plain language and gets a clear, multi-part answer built from that mission's facts.

3D game: a third-person astronaut explores a zone of exactly 20 × 20 meters around the mission's hardware. Gravity matches the chosen world, 3.71 m/s² on Mars and 1.62 m/s² on the Moon. Orbiters and probes that never landed are explored floating in the vacuum of space.

How it works: the mission data is stored in Python and sent to the browser. JavaScript builds the pages, runs the search, assistant and quiz, draws the space scene, and runs the game with WebGL. Photographs and their details are requested live from NASA's Image and Video Library. The search tolerates misspellings by measuring how closely the typed letters match each mission name (edit distance).

2. What benefits does it have?

Learning for all ages: the language targets high-school students and children under 18. Every idea is explained, then tested in the quiz, then seen in the photos and game.

Learning by doing: reading, asking, playing and exploring reinforce each other. In the game, a child can stand beside a lander and feel low gravity.

Honest storytelling: most websites celebrate launches. AUREX records how missions ended: a lost command, a dust storm, a deliberate impact.

Accessibility: it is free, needs no account, and works on a basic laptop and an Android phone with a touch joystick. It also respects reduced-motion settings.

Verifiable sources: every photograph links back to NASA's own record.

3. What is the intended impact?

The aim is to make mission history feel alive and to raise curiosity about space science, especially for students who may never visit a museum or university. A student who learns that Opportunity lasted about 14 years on a 90-day plan, or that Ranger 7 was built to crash, learns how engineers handle failure and uncertainty. We also hope it shows other young developers that a meaningful project can be built with free tools and a standard laptop.

4. What tools, coding languages, hardware and software were used?

HTML5 gives the structure: search, planet buttons, content areas and accessibility labels.

CSS3 handles the look: the glass-style panels, the Orbitron font, the status colors and the responsive layout. It also respects reduced-motion settings.

JavaScript (ES6+) provides the interaction: routing, fuzzy search, the assistant, the quiz generator and the photo pages. It also draws the space scene with Canvas 2D and runs the game.

Python 3 holds the mission data and serves it to the site using only its built-in libraries.

Three.js (WebGL) powers the 3D game.

NASA Image and Video Library API supplies the photographs and their details.

Hardware: an ordinary laptop and an Android phone for testing. No special equipment or paid software was used.

Use of AI: the source code was generated with the help of an AI assistant (Claude, by Anthropic), directed through detailed specifications from our team.

5. How is the project creative?

Original angle: it follows the afterlife of the hardware rather than only the launch.

Procedural space: nothing in the background is a stock image. The Milky Way, planets and moons are generated by code, with the planets in true order from the Sun.

Playable history: a child can walk beside a spacecraft instead of reading about it.

A small tutor in every mission: the assistant, quiz and explanation pages share the same facts, so each reinforces the others
